agencies.lines: Milwaukee County Transit System: CONNECT 1 bus rapid transit (rapid) and the bus routes that run every 15 minutes at the morning peak
Madison Metro: Rapid Route A (rapid transit), plus Routes B, C, D and 80, which like Route A run at least every 15 minutes on weekdays
Eau Claire Transit: Routes 9 and 19 run every 20 minutes, so they count only in the wider definitions

district.text: Every Wisconsin city with rail or rapid transit stops must zone a district where apartment buildings are allowed by right, at least 15 homes per acre, covering 15% of the land within ¼ mile of rail and rapid stops. The city picks the land. The model treats the district as spread at random over that land.

median_line.note: A median line of real cases is shown only when there are at least 4 comparable cases. Here the central line is already the average of the 11 district places, so no separate median line is shown.

scenarios.info: From our own lot-by-lot data on 11 US places that zoned a district for denser housing near some of their rail or rapid stops (on average about 12% of the land within ¼ mile). A model trained on lot and place traits (5 fits averaged) predicts what a 15% district, spread at random over Wisconsin's land within ¼ mile of rail and rapid stops, would add: about 450 extra homes over 2027–2031 (range about −120 to 820, refitting with one place left out at a time). The low end is below zero: no floor is set where the evidence does not set one. No model beat the plain average of the places on places it had not seen, so this is the low line, not the central one. The earlier little line, the station-area model for the broader law (43), is shown as a comparison.
scenarios.label: Little response
scenarios.source: Best lot model (lot + place traits, 5 averaged fits), Wisconsin within 1/4 mile: 449.6 extra homes over 2027-2031 (range -120.9 to 818.4), reference/tod_optiond_line.csv; New York pooled ramp

scenarios.info: The 11 places' average measured effect within ¼ mile of their reform stops, compared with similar stops without reform, before and after: about 33 extra new homes per 100 acres of lots a year. Applied to Wisconsin's lots within ¼ mile of rail and rapid stops (about 4,870 acres in Milwaukee and Madison, scaled to the state by homes near those stops, ×1.106) for five years: about 8,860 extra homes over 2027–2031 (range about 6,720 to 10,620, leaving out one place at a time). No model we tried beat this average on places it had not seen, so by the rule set before the results it is the central line. Caution: those cities chose their district land themselves, often land builders already wanted; a state mandate may do less. Land beyond ¼ mile counts zero. The earlier central line (the average reform city at the broader law's 71% coverage, 13,229) is shown as a comparison.
scenarios.label: Central: the average district place
scenarios.source: Average of the 11 district places' measured effect within 1/4 mile: 8,855.9 extra homes over 2027-2031 (range 6,715.3 to 10,624.4), reference/tod_optiond_line.csv; New York pooled ramp

scenarios.evidence: same 11 places, scaled to a 15% district
scenarios.info: The same 11 places, whose districts covered on average about 12% of the land within ¼ mile, less than the law's 15%. Scaling by the places' pooled effect per share of land zoned (their summed effects ÷ their summed district shares × 15%) gives about 11,060 extra homes over 2027–2031 (range about 8,050 to 14,840, leaving out one place at a time). This assumes a bigger district adds homes in proportion, which the places do not prove. The earlier strong line (Auckland's 2016 citywide upzoning, 17,148) is shown as a comparison.
scenarios.label: Strong: the average district place, scaled to 15%
scenarios.source: Average district place scaled to a 15% district by the pooled ratio: 11,057.3 extra homes over 2027-2031 (range 8,052.6 to 14,835.7), reference/tod_optiond_line.csv; New York pooled ramp

timing_caveat: The places' effects were measured over the years after each reform. The model places that effect inside 2027–2031, the law's first five years. Much of a real law's effect may come after 2031, so the yearly path is the least certain part of these numbers.
